subject: physics
question_text: Compare the isothermal process with the adiabatic process.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 Short Answer Question 8 (printed p.129). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: isothermal has ΔT = 0, PV = constant, ΔU = 0 so ΔQ = W; adiabatic has ΔQ = 0, PV^γ = constant, W = −ΔU; the adiabatic curve is the steeper of the two on a P–V diagram because γ = C_P/C_V is greater than 1.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The defining condition
lines: boundary at any stage, so ΔQ = 0.
steps.margin_note: First mark. State the defining condition of each process — ΔT = 0 for one, ΔQ = 0 for the other.
steps.why: These are the two DEFINING conditions — everything else in the comparison follows from one or the other.
common_mistakes: Saying the adiabatic process also has a constant temperature — the temperature changes; only the heat exchange is zero.
Confusing which symbol is held at zero for each process.

recall.must_convey: That isothermal means delta T equals zero and adiabatic means delta Q equals zero.
accept: delta T zero and delta Q zero

steps.memory_tip: Isothermal fixes the TEMPERATURE; adiabatic fixes the HEAT at zero.

steps.label: The P–V relation
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both relations, with γ named as C_P/C_V.
steps.why: Both processes obey the ideal gas equation of state; what differs is the extra POWER γ on V, which comes directly from ΔQ = 0.
common_mistakes: Writing PV^γ = constant for the isothermal process, or PV = constant for the adiabatic one.
Forgetting that γ is greater than 1, which is what makes the two curves different.

recall.must_convey: That isothermal obeys P V equals constant and adiabatic obeys P V to the gamma equals constant, with gamma greater than one.
accept: P V to the gamma equals constant
gamma is C P by C V

steps.memory_tip: The extra γ in PV^γ is what makes a process adiabatic instead of isothermal.

steps.label: The energy balance
lines: Isothermal: for an ideal gas U
depends only on T, so ΔU = 0 and
steps.margin_note: Third mark. State the energy balance of each process, not just its symbol.
steps.why: The energy balance is where the two processes differ most: one converts ALL its heat to work, the other converts none — it spends its own internal energy instead.
common_mistakes: Writing ΔU = 0 for the adiabatic process — the temperature, and so U, does change.
Mixing up which process has ΔQ = W and which has W = −ΔU.

recall.must_convey: That isothermal has delta U equal zero so delta Q equals W, and adiabatic has delta Q equal zero so W equals minus delta U.
accept: delta U zero delta Q equals W
delta Q zero W equals minus delta U
reject: P V to the gamma equals constant

steps.memory_tip: Isothermal: heat becomes work. Adiabatic: work comes out of the gas's own energy.

On a P–V diagram the adiabatic
curve is the steeper of the two,
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. State which container matches which process, and that adiabatic is the steeper curve.
steps.why: The container tells you WHY one process can hold T fixed and the other cannot — a slow process gives heat time to flow, a fast one does not.
common_mistakes: Saying the adiabatic curve is LESS steep than the isothermal — it is always the steeper of the two.
Swapping which container matches which process.

recall.must_convey: That isothermal is slow with a conducting container and adiabatic is fast with an insulated container, and the adiabatic curve is steeper because gamma is greater than one.
reject: delta U zero delta Q equals W

steps.memory_tip: Adiabatic is FAST and INSULATED; isothermal is SLOW and CONDUCTING. Adiabatic is also the steeper curve.

insider_note: Four contrasts, one mark each — an answer that only lists the two P–V relations and stops has written one of the four marks.
